newsitem.title: USA: Endangered condors released into wilds of Arizona.
newsitem.headline: Endangered condors released into wilds of Arizona.

text.p: Six young California condors were released into the wilds of northern Arizona on Thursday in an effort to re-establish the endangered scavenger birds in the area and ensure the rare bird's survival.
It was the first time that the giant birds -- the largest and rarest in North America -- had been seen in the skies of Arizona since 1924.
As about 400 onlookers watched from a mile (1.6 km) below, the birds were freed from holding pens on the 500-foot-high (152 metre) Vermilion Cliffs in an area near the Arizona-Utah border.
The six fledglings were soon testing their wings in the rugged and isolated terrain northeast of the Grand Canyon.
"All six of them came out and flew," said Hans Stuart, a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service spokesman. "It all went fine."
The release was witnessed by Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt who said: "This is the kind of story that clearly demonstrates that the Endangered Species Act works and works well."
Biologists are looking to establish a second independent population of condors in Arizona to go with one in California, where there have been seven such releases.
They said they will not be happy until they have 150 of the birds, including 15 breeding pairs, in each state.

There currently are 121 California condors in the world, with 104 in captivity and 17 released to the wild in southern California. The species had declined to just 21 birds, but was brought back from the brink of extinction with captive breeding programmes.

The California condor, with a 10-foot (3-metre) wingspan and weighing more than 20 pounds (9 kgs), is the largest land bird in North America and once flew over vast stretches of the West. The species is believed to be 11,000 years old, having soared during the last Ice Age, feasting on woolly mammoths and sabre-toothed tigers.

The birds released in Arizona were moved to their mountain top home in October from the Los Angeles Zoo and The World Centre for Birds of Prey in Boise, Idaho. They spent the last six weeks getting used to the surroundings and were kept away from humans.

Arizona offers wilder land with less human interference than southern California, and the Interior Department hopes to release more birds there on a yearly basis. Officials hope the condors will spread to the Grand Canyon and other areas.
